## 1. Intro and framework

- Tinder: mobile dating app
  - Shows a stack of profiles matching your preferences and near you
  - Swipe right = like, left = pass
  - Both swipe right: match; then they can DM
- Not an exact replica of an interview: more detail than you'd give live
- Framework: requirements → core entities → API → (no data flow; user-facing) → HLD (functional only) → deep dives (NFRs)

## 2. Functional requirements

- Ask how Tinder works and what the interviewer finds interesting; list features, prioritize for 35–45 minutes
1. **Set preferences**: age range, gender interest, max distance
   - Out of scope: full profile creation (photos, bio, prompts)
2. **View a stack of potential matches** matching preferences and within N miles of current location
3. **Swipe left (no) / right (yes)** on each profile
4. **Match notification** when both swipe right
- Constraint Evan often adds: **avoid showing repeat profiles** (already decided on them)

## 3. Non-functional requirements

- Steps: pick qualities relevant to this system, put them in context, quantify
  - The site's delivery framework page lists qualities to consider
- **CAP: consistency for swipes**, availability elsewhere
  - The second person to swipe right gets an instant match screen
  - Needs the latest writes: the other person may have swiped moments before
  - Caveat: there's a way to skip this (deep dive)
- **Low-latency stack loading: < 300 ms**
  - Filtering by location + preferences can be slow without care
  - ~200 ms feels real time ("a blink"); aim 200–500 ms
- **Scale: 10M DAU; high write throughput**
  - 10M × ~100 swipes/day, plus peaks

## 4. Core entities

- Communicate that the full schema comes in the HLD
- **Profile** (with preferences), **Swipe**, **Match**

## 5. API

```
POST /profiles        body: { minAge, maxAge, gender, radius, ... } -> 200 | Profile
GET  /stack?lat&long  -> Profile[]
POST /swipes/:userId  body: { decision: yes | no } -> Match?
```

- Current location passed as query params: it changes, not just stored
- **Never put the caller's userId in path/query/body**: easy to forge (see others' stacks)
  - Use a JWT or session token in the header; the server derives the user
- Swipe path param = the *other* user
- Match push notification is server-initiated: no user-facing API

## 6. HLD: profiles and preferences

- Client (mobile) → **API gateway** (microservices; routing, plus auth, rate limiting) → **profile service** → **profile DB**
  - If unsure, microservices are the most common choice in SD interviews
- Profile: name, minAgePref, maxAgePref, genderPref, maxDistance, …
  - Schema defined here, next to the DB, as fields come up
- DB choice doesn't matter much: little data, few relations
- Example insert (you'd never write this live)

```sql
INSERT INTO profile (name, min_age, max_age, gender_pref, max_distance)
VALUES ('Evan', 25, 35, 'female', 10);
```

## 7. HLD: the stack

- Profile service: query 1 gets the user's preferences; query 2 finds matching profiles
  - Filter by age, gender, and distance from passed lat/long
- Correction: we do store each user's latest location (on each stack request) to compare against others
- Inefficient: lat/long indexes are 1-D for 2-D data; big scans; fix later
- "Should I start simple if I know the answer?"
  - You can mention a geospatial index if you know it
  - Starting simple helps when you don't know yet, and stops you burning 20 minutes early
  - Common failure: deep-diving here and never meeting the other requirements

## 8. HLD: swipes (and why Cassandra)

- Separate **swipe service**: very different traffic (~100 swipes per stack fetch); scale independently
- Separate **swipe DB**
  - "One DB per microservice" is overly pedantic and outdated; services can share DBs
  - Separate here because the requirements differ: very write-heavy
- Math
  - 10M × 100 = **1B swipes/day**
  - ÷ ~100K s/day = **~10K/s average** (he first said 100K, then corrected)
  - × ~10 for peaks (late-night swiping, seasonality) = **~100K writes/s peak**
- Swipe row: user1, user2, liked (yes/no), createdAt; **< 100 bytes**
- Postgres on a big AWS instance: roughly **5K–20K writes/s per node** (depends on data, instance; rough)
  - 5–20 nodes would work
- **Cassandra** handles the same with fewer nodes (Netflix tech blog: linear scaling, 1M writes/s)
  - Trade-off: two DB technologies for the team vs more Postgres cost
- Why Cassandra writes are faster (hand-wavy)
  1. Append to the commit log (disk)
  2. Write to the **memtable** (memory)
  3. Acknowledge
  4. Periodically flush memory to disk as an **append** to a file; **compaction** merges later
- Postgres
  1. Append to the **write-ahead log** (disk)
  2. Write to the DB on disk: seek the right page, find/update the row
  - Some caching optimizations exist ("I can hear you yelling in the comments")
- Essence: Cassandra batches writes and appends

## 9. HLD: matches and notifications

- On a right swipe: write the swipe, check for the inverse swipe
- If found: create a **Match** (user1, user2, createdAt)
  - Evan puts it in the profile DB (future: load a profile and its matches); not the crux
- Second swiper gets the match synchronously in the response
- First swiper gets a **push notification** via **APNs** (Apple) or **FCM** (Firebase, Android)

## 10. Deep dive: consistent swipes

- Proactivity by level
  - Mid-level: interviewer may drive with "how do you keep swipes consistent?"; it's about problem solving
  - Senior: lead 1–2 deep dives at good depth
  - Staff: fully proactive, deep in 2–3 places
  - Staff caution: don't monologue; it's still a conversation
    - "Here are my three priorities; would you reorder?" lets the interviewer steer to what they want to see
- Problem: Cassandra is **eventually consistent** by default
  - A and B swipe right at nearly the same time
  - Each writes, then checks the inverse; the replica hasn't seen the other write
  - Neither gets a sync match; no async notification either; the match is lost forever
- **Option 1: don't be consistent**
  - First swiper never knows when the other swiped
  - Hourly reconciliation job finds missed matches and notifies both asynchronously
  - Keeps Cassandra, cheaper; staff candidates often argue this
  - Interviewers often push back ("handle the consistency anyway"); raise it, be ready
- **Option 2: keep Cassandra, add Redis**
  - Cassandra's stronger consistency settings still leave gaps and blunt its write advantage
  - Redis key `user1:user2` (ordered = user1 liked user2), value anything (e.g., true)
  - On swipe: write my key and check the inverse **atomically**
    - Redis is single-threaded with atomic operations: read/write can't interleave
  - Then write the swipe to Cassandra
  - New problem: Redis + Cassandra = **distributed transaction**
    - Mention the **Saga pattern** for consistent distributed transactions
  - Redis is fast but costly at size; partition by user
    - Reciprocal keys must land on the same node: partition by the sorted pair
  - Write-up version: one key `swipes:123:456` holding both users' decisions (write-up)
- **Option 3: drop Cassandra, use Postgres**
  - 5–20 nodes; ACID transactions built in
  - One row per pair: user1, user2, user1Decision, user2Decision
  - Upsert locks the row; the second writer waits, then sees the like and triggers the match
  - Higher cost; no Redis needed
- Write-up option: **Cassandra single-partition transactions** (write-up)
  - Partition key `user_pair` = sorted "smaller:larger"; both directions in one partition

```sql
CREATE TABLE swipes (
  user_pair text, from_user uuid, to_user uuid, direction text, created_at timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_pair), from_user, to_user));
```

- Verdict: Cassandra + Redis or the Postgres row design are both "five out of five"
  - Staff: show this depth; senior: land on one and explain it; mid-level: "check a cache" is fine without the distributed-transaction nuance

## 11. Deep dive: low-latency stack loading

- Problem: two queries, and the location filter is 2-D; loading spinner while you want love
- **Geo-sharding alone**: falls short
  - Users travel; boundary users (NY vs NJ) need other shards; dense areas (NYC) stay slow
- **Precompute** (like feeds)
  - Nightly (or every 6 h) cron runs the expensive query per user into a **stack cache**; reads are O(1)
  - Stale when: profiles deleted, user moves (Seattle → LA), preferences change
    - Invalidate affected caches (complex logic); refresh or accept a slow load
  - Finishing the cached stack still triggers the slow query
- **Fix the root cause: geospatial index**
  - Option A: **Postgres + PostGIS** extension
    - Some say it doesn't scale; we're well within limits; Evan would likely choose this
  - Option B: **Elasticsearch** (native geo queries), synced via **CDC** (Postgres events → Kafka, or DynamoDB Streams → consumer)
  - Prefers PostGIS: no new data store to learn and run
- **Best: combine**
  - Cron precomputes from the geo index; cache misses/invalidations query the index directly
  - Prefetch: at the 90th of 100 profiles, load the next batch so the stack feels infinite
- See the Uber video for geospatial index details

## 12. Deep dive: scale

- Hand-waved: scale services horizontally, shard DBs, partition caches, managed Elasticsearch clusters, load balancers

## 13. Deep dive: no repeat profiles

- Simplest: load the stack, query everything the user swiped on, remove in memory
  - Fine for mid-level; inefficient
- **Cache a set per user**: key = user, value = set of swiped user IDs
  - Size: 10M × 100/day × ~100 B × 365 ≈ **36.5 TB/year**
  - Big caches are ~128 GB; most AWS caches 32–64 GB: lots of instances, expensive
- **Index on user1** in the swipe DB: makes the query fast; "probably the simplest, maybe the best"
- **Bloom filter**
  - Space-efficient, probabilistic set membership
  - False positives possible, no false negatives
  - On "maybe seen," confirm against the DB
  - Evan: slight over-engineering; still large; prefetching hides the index cost
- **Staff move: push back on the constraint**
  - Re-show profiles after ~30 days (or 60, 90)
  - Clear the cache after 30 days; arguably better UX (people and profiles change)
  - Like pushing back on a PM's requirement at work, for users and cost
- Write-up labels: DB query + contains (bad); cache + DB + contains (great); cache + contains + Bloom filter (great) (write-up)

## 14. What is expected at each level

- Not all of this is expected from mid-level or even senior; Evan went deep everywhere
- Write-up bars (write-up)
  - E4: clear API and data model; working HLD for feed, swipes, matches; traditional + geo filters; avoid re-showing swiped profiles
  - E5: speed through HLD; discuss feed generation and match creation in detail; know a fitting index; know when feed caches go stale
  - Staff: depth everywhere, may steer elsewhere; trade-offs like a peer

## 15. Board as text (assembled from the talk)

```
Mobile -> API GW -> Profile Service -> Profile DB (Postgres + PostGIS)
                        |     ^            | CDC -> Elasticsearch (geo)
                        |     +-- Stack cache <- cron precompute / prefetch
                        |
                    Swipe Service -> Redis (atomic "a:b" + check "b:a")
                        |        -> Swipe DB (Cassandra)
                        +-> Match -> APNs / FCM push (first swiper)
```

- Alternatives on the board: Postgres pair-row with row locks; reconciliation cron; Bloom filter; 30-day re-show
